11729-life-of-johnson-volume-6-addenda-i:
George Birkbeck Hill edited this sixth volume of Boswell's Life of Johnson in 1887, adding addenda, an index, and dicta philosophi. It also includes Boswell's journal of a tour to the Hebrides and Johnson's diary of a journey into North Wales, in six volumes overall.

Titles of works quoted in the notes open the book, from Addison's works to memoirs of Rockingham and correspondence of John Wilkes. Addenda bring autograph letters, and the index runs from pronunciation and property to puns, which Johnson despised yet made himself. The volume is a scholar's apparatus, closing a great biography with tools for its readers.
15219-if-only-etc:
F. C. Philips's 1904 Leipzig volume gathers stories, songs, and sketches under the title If Only, etc. Contents include If Only, One Can't Always Tell, songs after Hugo and other French poets, a piece on love and money, and a puzzled painter written with Augustus Harris. A dedication honors Sydney Grundy, his old collaborator.

The title story opens on free will, arguing that surroundings, fate, and circumstance shape even a man's choice of wife. Philips writes in a light, worldly style, mixing wit with moral reflection. Readers of Edwardian light fiction will find the collection varied, amusing, and pleasantly old-fashioned.
26492-studies-of-american-fungi-mushroom:
George Francis Atkinson, professor of botany at Cornell, published this study of American fungi in a second edition, copyrighted in 1900 and 1901. Two hundred and thirty illustrations from the author's photographs, with colored plates by F. R. Rathbun, show the more important genera of agarics found in the United States. Sarah Tyson Rorer adds recipes for cooking mushrooms, and J. F. Clark writes on their chemistry and toxicology.

Species entries give size, shape, color, and habitat, with plain judgments of edible or poisonous. Pluteus cervinus, for example, stands seven to fifteen centimeters high, with a cap five to ten broad, growing from rotten wood and stumps from spring to late autumn. The book grew from Cornell experiment station bulletins into a standard field guide.
30597-the-battle-of-atlanta-and-other-ca:
Major-General Grenville M. Dodge writes The Battle of Atlanta and Other Campaigns, Addresses, and related pieces, published in Council Bluffs, Iowa, in 1911. A frontispiece shows Dodge as commander of the Department of the Missouri in 1865.

Contents move from the southwestern campaign and a letter to his father to the Battle of Atlanta and a letter to General Raum. Indian campaigns of 1864 to 1866, a campaign up the Tennessee River valley, the Army of the Tennessee, and the campaign in the West follow. Talks to old comrades, a piece on General Grant, block houses in war, and an incident of war close the volume.
33815-the-wisdom-of-confucius-with-criti:
Epiphanius Wilson presents the wisdom of Confucius with critical and biographical sketches in this Art Type Edition of the World's Popular Classics, copyrighted in 1900. Twenty books of sayings move from learning and miscellaneous sayings through good government, filial piety, and the superior man, to abuses of propriety in ceremony and music, social virtue, the golden rule.

Further books give sayings of Tsang, a favorite disciple's opinion of the master, Confucius in private and official life, comparative worth of disciples, answers on governing and consistency. The volume also adds sayings of Mencius and the Shi-King odes. It offers English readers a compact, readable entry to classical Chinese thought.
35162-gullible-s-travels-etc:
Ring W Lardner wrote these comic tales, printed by the Bobbs-Merrill Company of Indianapolis with a 1917 copyright. May Wilson Preston drew the pictures. Lardner had won his name with You Know Me Al. A plate begs that towels be put in room 559. The set holds Carmen, Three Kings and a Pair, the title tale, The Water Cure, and Three Without, Doubled.

Carmen opens at a rummy game at Hatch's, where Hatch has all the luck and the teller's wife plays like she was bought off. The pair settle seven and a half down. Hatch pours the kitchen beer and, his best friend could not say, gives himself the worst of it. Lardner's voice runs in the rough speech of his ballpark world.
42890-the-paris-sketch-book-of-mr-m-a-ti:
The Paris Sketch Book and The Irish Sketch Book, by William Makepeace Thackeray, were issued together in London in 1902. Thackeray used the pen name Titmarsh for the Paris pieces. He drew the pictures himself. Paris heads treat an invasion of France and a caution to travellers. Essays take up French painting, novels, and drama. Tales such as The Painter's Bargain and A Gambler's Death sit among them.

The Irish part runs to near thirty chapters of travel. Thackeray moves from Dublin through Cork, Killarney, Galway, and Belfast. He visits convents, shows, races, and petty sessions. Father Mathew and the Giant's Causeway both appear. The pair of books shows his sharp eye for manners, folly, and local colour on both sides of the sea.
48343-clergymen-and-doctors-curious-fact:
Clergymen and Doctors, issued in Edinburgh in Nimmo's Series of Commonplace Books, gathers curious facts and short sketches about two professions that Victorian readers loved to gossip over. No author is named; the book is a commonplace collection, sorted by name and topic rather than told as one story. Its pages run from archbishops to apothecaries.

The contents list hundreds of small items. Readers meet Abernethy and the Duke of York, learn what an archdeacon is, and hear of Bishop Berkeley's Bermuda scheme and Queen Elizabeth's blood-jewels. A long run of entries sorts doctors' fees across the ages, from early English practice to large royal payments. George Crabbe appears as the apothecary poet, and Da Vinci as a great anatomist. Jokes from pulpits sit beside tales of fees refused with style. Readers get a browsing book of anecdotes, best taken a few pages at a time.
50958-representative-women-of-deseret-a-:
Augusta Joyce Crocheron compiled and wrote Representative Women of Deseret, a book of biographical sketches. J C Graham and Company printed it at Salt Lake City in 1884. The book accompanies a picture bearing the same title. Crocheron, author of Wild Flowers of Deseret, dedicated both to the women portrayed, their co-laborers in the Church, and every true heart. The picture stands for the Latter Day Saints women's organizations rather than for gifts of mind.

The women were chosen by the precedence they hold in those organizations. Salt Lake City is the head of the work, so its laborers stand first. The sketches aim to acquaint strangers with their labors and virtues. They show, as it were, what manner of people these Mormons are. A second work was promised in due season.
51090-a-polyglot-of-foreign-proverbs-com:
A Polyglot of Foreign Proverbs, by Henry G Bohn, was printed in London by the author house at York Street, Covent Garden, in 1857. The book holds French, Italian, German, Dutch, Spanish, Portuguese, and Danish proverbs, with English versions and a general index.

In his preface Bohn says that while editing his Handbook of English Proverbs, the idea came to him. A collection of foreign proverbs, arranged in monographs and brought into match by a general index, would interest the ordinary reader and the linguist alike. More than one reviewer of the Handbook suggested nearly the same idea. After more than two years of patient labour, he presents his gleanings. He hopes they will not be found deficient of grain. Saying fans get seven nations wisdom in one shelf book.
51107-woman-and-puppet-etc:
Pierre Louÿs wrote Woman and Puppet, translated and adapted by G F Monkshood, issued in London by Greening and Company in nineteen oh eight. Monkshood gave the book to John W White, painter of beautiful things. Seven pieces fill the volume. Woman and Puppet stands first and longest. A translator note recalls Oscar Wilde dedication of Salome to Louÿs some twelve years before.

At that time few in England knew the name of the writer who would grow famous as author of Aphrodite, the note says. About ten years ago all the republic of French letters praised Aphrodite, it adds. It was the most amazing study of antiquity since Flaubert Salambo, the note holds. The New Pleasure, Byblis, Lêda, and Immortal Love follow in the volume. The Artist Triumphant and The Hill of Horsel close it. Readers get Louÿs lush, pagan tales in English dress.
52642-a-lear-of-the-steppes-etc:
Ivan Turgenev wrote A Lear of the Steppes, here in Constance Garnett's translation, issued in 1906 as volume twelve of the Novels of Ivan Turgenev. An essay fronts the tale and praises its build: the story, it says, is so fine in structure and so strong in effect that it exposes how artificial most clever fiction is. It grows, the essay argues, from the roots of life itself.

The essay singles out Turgenev's way in: Harlov, the Lear of the story, is brought forward with such force on the threshold that every eye must follow him. Around him stand his household, his two daughters, and a crowd of figures, each living by the laws of his own being. The narrator tells the tale as his memories, with seeming carelessness that hides the art. Readers get a Turgenev tale with a guide to why it works placed before it.
53959-sir-ian-hamilton-s-despatches-from:
Sir Ian Hamilton's Despatches from the Dardanelles prints the official reports of the Gallipoli campaign's commander, issued by George Newnes in London. Field Marshal Sir Evelyn Wood wrote the introduction. The contents list the first despatch, the second despatch, press bureau statements, and a despatch from Vice Admiral de Robeck, with five maps among the illustrations.

Wood opens by recalling gallant deeds he has witnessed across sixty one years. He begins with the first Victoria Cross ever gazetted, won by a naval lieutenant who threw a live shell overboard. He ends with the ladder party at the Great Redan before Sevastopol. Against that standard of fighting values, he presents Hamilton's account of the Dardanelles fighting.
57192-principle-in-art-etc:
Coventry Patmore wrote Principle in Art, Etc., a set of essays printed in London in 1889. Contents list twenty-five pieces. The title essay stands first, then real apprehension, and seers, thinkers, and talkers. Possibilities and performances, cheerfulness in life and art, and the point of rest in art follow. Fancy, pathos, and the wholeness of poems take their turns. The bounds of genius and love and poetry close the first run.

Single poets then take whole essays: Keats, Shelley, Blake, and Rossetti among them. Shall Smith have a statue stands among the later heads. Building takes the last essays, on ideal and material greatness in building, old English building old and new, and building styles. The first essay holds that it is not true that fault-finding is of no use to art. To judge, it says, asks a judge's training, not mere feeling for beauty.
61513-the-phantom-death-etc:
W Clark Russell's sea tales fill The Phantom Death, Etc. Press notices from many papers front the book. The Manchester Courier praises its salt air at length. The Lazarette of the Huntress earns its top praise. Ten more yarns stand beside that tale. The Sun finds not one dull piece among them.

The Speaker ranks the book with Russell's best work. The Daily Telegraph calls the tales first-class all through. Horror, the grotesque, and humor mix in them, one paper says. No writer knows the moods of the sea like Russell, says another. Lloyd's Weekly News finds them capital reading. Sea yarns of ghosts, wrecks, and strange deaths made Russell the sailor's novelist, and this set gathers his shorter work for armchair crews.
62225-battlefield-church-salop-an-histor:
Fletcher, vicar of a Shrewsbury parish, wrote a short guide to the church at Battlefield for its many visitors. The Shrewsbury Journal offices printed it in 1889, from pieces that had run in that paper. A preface thanks the incumbent who asked for the work. Fletcher says he found new facts in the Public Record Office.

Battlefield Church owes its start to the victory of Henry the Fourth at the battle of Shrewsbury. The book tells that fight, then the founding of the church and its college of priests. It gives the will of Roger Ive, a list of the masters, and the story of the college's fall. A full account of the fabric follows, its size, tower, windows, and bells. The images of Our Lady of Pity and the Corbet monument are treated in turn, and the repairs of 1749 and 1861 close the survey.
69528-nuts-to-crack-a-galaxy-of-puzzles-:
A tiny monthly magazine of puzzles, the Multum in Parvo Library's volume two, number twenty, dated August 1895, calls itself the smallest magazine in the world. Subscriptions cost fifty cents a year, single copies five cents. A B Courtney published it from Milk Street, Boston. Two puzzling queries open the number. Read the surprising sentence All 0, it challenges: the answer is nothing after all.

Make one word of the letters of new door, it continues: the answer is one word itself. A grammatical puzzle follows. Such pocket puzzle papers fed the Victorian craze for riddles, rebuses, and word play. Answers are printed upside into the fun.
76651-happy-days-carolings-of-colorado-e:
Sam Brown wrote these poems, Happy Days and Carolings of Colorado. Reed printed the book at Denver in 1904. Brown gives it with kind regards to a summer tourist guest. A publishers sketch of his life opens the small volume.

Brown was born in the South Platte valley near Denver town. Bison and prong horn antelope ranged the plains in his boyhood. Indian papooses were his earliest playmates on the wild frontier there. Cheyenne Charley, Black Kettle, and Colorow stand in his memory still. Overland stage coaches and ox teams crowd his youthful memory of the plains days.
doe-osti-3375576-producing-cultivated-me:
A CRADA final report numbered LBNL-2001765, dated June 9, 2026, covers work with Novel Farms, Inc. on cultivated meat. Melanie Sonsteng of Lawrence Berkeley Lab was the technical contact. Michelle Lu served for the firm. Novel Farms came through the Cyclotron Road program for lab-based founders. The firm grows animal cells on its own scaffold sheets. It hopes to make real meat cuts that cost no more than farm-raised meat.

Cost is the wall in this field. The growth factors in cell feed media cost far too much at scale. The firm's scaffold aims to cut that bill. It gives cells a three-dimensional home laced with the proteins they use to grip, grow, and mature. The project tuned how well the scaffold serves a range of animal cell lines. Funding came through the nonprofit Activate, not the Energy Department. No papers or patents came out of the work.
if-only-etc:
F. C. Philips, author of As in a Looking Glass, issued this Leipzig volume in 1904. It holds a title tale, If Only, a short piece called One Can't Always Tell, and songs after French poets. One playlet was written with Sir Augustus Harris. Philips dedicated the book to Sydney Grundy.

The title tale opens on free will and fate in marriage. Its speaker holds that chance and the acts of others shape a life more than choice. Later pieces turn lighter, with love, money, and a puzzled painter. The book mixes a grave tale with brief stage and verse work.
life-of-johnson-volume-6-addenda-index-d:
Volume Six closes Hill's Boswell with addenda and an index. Its contents list titles of works quoted in the notes. Autograph letters and other additions supplement the main life. A section of Dicta Philosophi gathers Johnson's sayings.

Hill admits his list of quoted works is not fully complete. Dates show the editions he used, not first publications. Poets are mostly omitted, since references fit all editions equally. The volume serves scholars checking Boswell's vast web of references. Addison's works, in six volumes of 1862, head the reference list. Almon's Wilkes correspondence and Arrighi's Paoli history follow alphabetically.
podcast-joerogan-EGJ1hyYmmTc:
Graham Hancock and Randall Carlson appear together on episode 1897 of the Joe Rogan Experience, a pairing fans of ancient mysteries treat as a main event. Hancock argues a lost ice-age civilization taught the ancient world. Carlson, a geologist by training, backs the catastrophe side of the case.

Together they lay out their evidence: flood myths, old monuments, and signs of a comet strike near the end of the last ice age. Rogan referees and marvels by turns. The episode is the duo's fullest joint statement on the show, a long, detailed brief for a past far stranger than the textbooks allow.
podcast-joerogan-llgBlytRttc:
Rick Doblin's latest Rogan sit-down, episode 2319 of the Joe Rogan Experience, updates his life's work. Doblin founded MAPS to make MDMA a legal medicine. By this visit the therapy stood at the edge of approval, with regulators holding the final word.

He tells Rogan what the last push requires, how clinics would train therapists, and what he fears from a rushed rollout. Rogan asks the veteran campaigner to look back down the forty-year road. The episode is a status report from the hopeful end of a long fight, by the man who never left it.
podcast-joerogan-pCH-R3L6QTc:
Comedian Joe DeRosa returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2538. DeRosa is a regular in Rogan's circle of comics. His humor runs dark, dry, and self-aware.

The pair trade stories from clubs, tours, and years on the road. DeRosa shares his takes on food, fandom, and the grind of stand-up. Rogan knows his act well, so the talk stays loose. Fans of either man get the feel of two old friends recording the chat they would have had anyway, microphones or not. Their ease marks years of shared rooms and roads.
podcast-joerogan-uk2h9oBZctc:
Comedian Ali Siddiq joins Joe Rogan for episode 2523. Siddiq is famed as a storyteller who builds long tales from his Houston life. Prison years sit inside many of his best bits.

Rogan gives him room to spin stories at his own pace. Each tale lands with a laugh and a hard truth. They talk about craft, timing, and respect among comics. The episode is a master class in stand-up storytelling. Fans leave with a clear sense of why peers rank Siddiq among the best live acts working today. His timing turns hard years into warm laughs.
tieck-tales-from-the-phantasus-etc:
Ludwig Tieck practically invented the German Romantic tale, and the Phantasus gathered his best early work. Tales from the Phantasus presents selections in English: fairy tales, haunted legends, and dreamlike stories framed as friends telling tales to one another. Eerie and witty by turns, the pieces defy easy summary.

Blond Eckbert's paranoia, the Runenberg's mountain lure, and other strange fancies show Romanticism discovering the uncanny inside ordinary life. Tieck moves between folk simplicity and polished irony without breaking stride. English readers get the movement's master storyteller in accessible form. These tales shaped how Germany imagined the marvelous for a century. They still read like dreams remembered at breakfast.
